title: Java basics, classes, references, recursion, IntLists
summary: What a Java variable actually holds, what = really does, how static differs from instance, and how a list can be built from small objects pointing at each other. Almost every “what would Java print”, box-and-pointer and linked-list coding question on the final rests on this unit.

lesson.title: How a Java program is put together

blocks.text: Java is statically typed: every variable and expression has a type that the compiler knows before the program runs. All code lives inside classes. Execution starts at public static void main(String[] args).
A blueprint. It declares instance variables (one copy per object), static variables (one copy total), constructors and methods.
A thing built from a class with new. Each object has its own copy of every instance variable.
The method with the class’s name and no return type; it runs when new Dog(5) is evaluated.

A compile error is found by javac from types alone; nothing runs at all. A runtime error (exception) happens while the program runs, e.g. NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, ClassCastException, StackOverflowError.
Small facts that decide many print questions:

items: Integer division truncates toward zero: 7 / 2 is 3, -7 / 2 is −3. The remainder takes the sign of the left operand: -7 % 3 is −1, 5 % -3 is 2.
Casting a double to int truncates toward zero: (int) -3.99 is −3.
char is a number: 'a' + 1 is the int 98, (char) ('a' + 1) is b, 'b' - 'a' is 1.
+ is evaluated left to right; once a String is involved, the rest is concatenation: 1 + 2 + "3" + 4 + 5 is "3345", "x" + 'a' + 1 is "xa1", but 'a' + 1 + "x" is "98x".

blocks.title: Arithmetic and concatenation
steps: 7 / 2: both ints, truncate 3.5 → 3. This happens before any String appears, so it is real arithmetic.
-7 % 3: −7 = 3·(−2) + (−1), remainder keeps the sign of −7 → −1.
'a' + 1 inside parentheses: char + int = int, 97 + 1 = 98.

blocks.text: Type errors are compile errors even on lines that would never execute. int x = "hi"; anywhere in the file means the program never runs.
Instance members belong to one object; static members belong to the class, so there is exactly one copy shared by everything.

head: Instance
Static
rows: no this; cannot touch instance variables without an object

blocks.name: Static access through an instance
blocks.text: Writing d2.binomen = "Lupus" is legal, but it writes the single static variable Dog.binomen. Every object (and the class) then reads "Lupus".

blocks.name: Default values
blocks.text: Fields (instance and static) start as 0, 0.0, false, '\u0000', or null. Local variables have no default: reading one before assigning is a compile error.

blocks.title: Static counter and a shared name
blocks.prompt: Dog has int weight, id; String name; static int count = 0; static String binomen; and the constructor does weight = w; count += 1; id = count;. Run Dog d1 = new Dog(5), d2 = new Dog(30); d1.name = "Fido"; Dog.binomen = "Canis"; d2.binomen = "Lupus"; then print d1.binomen, Dog.binomen, d1.name, d2.name, d1.count, d1.id, d2.id.
steps: Constructing d1: count becomes 1, d1.id = 1. Constructing d2: count becomes 2, d2.id = 2.
Dog.binomen = "Canis" then d2.binomen = "Lupus": both write the same single static box, which now holds "Lupus".
d1.binomen and Dog.binomen both read that box: Lupus Lupus.
d1.name is "Fido"; d2.name was never assigned so it is null.
d1.count is just another spelling of Dog.count = 2. The ids were copied at construction time: 1 and 2.

blocks.text: Inside a static method, using an instance variable (weight) or this is a compile error: “non-static variable cannot be referenced from a static context”.

lesson.title: Primitives, references and the Golden Rule of Equals

blocks.text: A variable is a box of bits. Java has 8 primitive types (byte, short, int, long, float, double, boolean, char): the box holds the value. Everything else (arrays, Strings, all classes) is a reference type: the box holds an address (an arrow) or null.

blocks.name: Golden Rule of Equals (GRoE)
blocks.text: y = x copies the bits in box x into box y. For a primitive that is an independent copy of the value; for a reference it is a copy of the arrow, so both names now lead to the same object.

blocks.name: Parameter passing is GRoE (pass by value)
blocks.text: Calling f(x) copies x’s bits into the parameter. A method can mutate the object a reference points to, but it can never make the caller’s variable point somewhere else.

blocks.title: What would Java print: aliasing vs copying
blocks.prompt: int x = 5; int y = x; y = 10; Walrus a = new Walrus(1000); Walrus b = a; b.weight = 5; Print x, y, a.weight, b.weight.
steps: y = x copies the value 5; then y is overwritten with 10. x is unaffected: 5 10.
b = a copies the address: one walrus, two arrows.
b.weight = 5 means “follow b’s arrow and change that object”. a follows the same arrow.

blocks.title: Mutation through a parameter, then re-aiming
blocks.prompt: static int[] fiddle(int[] a, int[] b) { a[0] = b[1]; b = a; b[1] = 42; a = new int[]{9, 9}; return b; } With int[] fa = {1, 2}, fb = {3, 4}; int[] fr = fiddle(fa, fb); print fa, fb, fr and fr == fa.
steps: Inside, a → fa’s array, b → fb’s array (copied arrows).
a[0] = b[1]: fa’s array becomes {4, 2}.
b = a: the local b now also points at fa’s array (fb in main is untouched).
b[1] = 42: fa’s array becomes {4, 42}.
a = new int[]{9, 9}: re-aims the local a only; nobody returns it, so it becomes garbage.
Return b, i.e. fa’s array.
blocks.answer: fa = [4, 42], fb = [3, 4], fr = [4, 42], fr == fa is true.

blocks.text: “Java passes objects by reference” is the wrong model. Java passes everything by value; for objects the value is an arrow. Assigning to a parameter never affects the caller.
== on references asks “same address?”. Two separate arrays with equal contents are not ==. Use Arrays.equals or .equals for contents.

lesson.title: Box-and-pointer diagrams and arrays of references

blocks.title: Drawing a box-and-pointer diagram
items: For every variable draw a labeled box. Primitive: write the value inside. Reference: draw an arrow (or a slash for null).
For every new, draw the object with its own field boxes, and an arrow from wherever the address is stored.
For every assignment, copy exactly what is in the right-hand box: a number, or an arrow to the same place.
An object no arrow reaches is garbage: cross it out; it can never be reached again.

blocks.text: An array is an object: a fixed number of numbered boxes of one type plus a length field (no parentheses). new int[3] gives zeros; new Dog[3] gives three null arrows and builds no dogs. A 2D array is an array of arrows to arrays: rows can have different lengths and can even be the same array.

blocks.title: Box-and-pointer: a 2D array with a shared row
blocks.prompt: int[][] m = new int[3][]; m[0] = new int[]{1}; m[1] = new int[]{2, 3}; m[2] = m[1]; m[2][0] = 9; Draw the diagram and print m[1][0], m[1] == m[2], m.length.
steps: new int[3][]: one outer array with three slots, all null (rows not built yet).
m[0] → a new array [1]; m[1] → a new array [2, 3].
m[2] = m[1] copies the arrow: slots 1 and 2 point at the same row.
m[2][0] = 9 follows that arrow: the shared row becomes [9, 3].
Diagram: m → [ • | • | • ]; slot 0 → [1]; slots 1 and 2 → the same [9 | 3].

blocks.title: Arrays of references and clone
blocks.prompt: Dog[] dogs = new Dog[3]; dogs[0] = new Dog(10); dogs[1] = dogs[0]; dogs[2] = new Dog(20); dogs[1].weight = 99; Dog[] copy = dogs.clone(); copy[2] = dogs[1]; copy[0].weight++; Print dogs[0].weight, dogs[2].weight, copy[2].weight, copy == dogs, copy[0] == dogs[0].
steps: dogs: slot 0 → Dog A(10), slot 1 → the same Dog A, slot 2 → Dog B(20).
dogs[1].weight = 99 changes Dog A: A.weight = 99.
clone() makes a new array whose slots are copies of the arrows (a shallow copy): copy → [A, A, B].
copy[2] = dogs[1] re-aims only copy’s slot 2 to A; dogs[2] still → B.
copy[0].weight++ follows to A: 100.
copy and dogs are different arrays (false) whose slot 0 holds the same arrow (true).

blocks.text: String[] s = new String[2]; s[0].length() compiles but throws NullPointerException: the slot holds null, there is no object to follow.
A recursive method solves a problem by trusting itself on a smaller instance. It needs a base case answered directly and a recursive case that makes progress toward it.

blocks.name: Leap of faith
blocks.text: Assume the recursive call returns the correct answer for the smaller input; check only that (1) the base case is right, (2) you build the full answer correctly from the smaller answer, (3) every call moves toward a base case. Correctness then follows by induction.
Each call gets its own stack frame with its own parameters and locals. Missing or skippable base cases cause StackOverflowError.

blocks.title: Trace a recursion tree
blocks.prompt: static int f(int n) { if (n <= 1) return 1; return f(n - 1) + f(n - 2); } What are f(4) and f(5)?
steps: f(0) = f(1) = 1 (base cases).
f(5) = f(4) + f(3) = 8. Note f(2) is recomputed many times: this recursion makes exponentially many calls.

blocks.title: Recursing over an array with a helper index
blocks.prompt: Write static int sum(int[] a, int i) returning a[i] + … + a[a.length − 1]; evaluate sum(new int[]{4, 1, 5}, 0).
steps: Base case: if i >= a.length the suffix is empty, return 0.
Recursive case: return a[i] + sum(a, i + 1);

blocks.text: A base case the input can skip over is as bad as none: if (n == 0) return 0; return n + g(n - 2); recurses forever on odd n. Use n <= 0. With that fix, g(7) = 7 + 5 + 3 + 1 + 0 = 16 using 5 calls.
L = new IntList(5, null); L = new IntList(10, L); L = new IntList(15, L); builds 15 → 10 → 5: each new node goes in front, its rest pointing at the old list.
Builds new nodes and leaves the input unchanged (calls new once per output node).
Changes the existing nodes (their first or rest) and calls new zero times.

blocks.title: Destructive vs non-destructive
blocks.prompt: L = [15 10 5]. Run IntList M = incrList(L, 2); then IntList N = dincrList(L, 1);. What are L, M, N and is N == L?
steps: incrList makes 3 new nodes holding 17, 12, 7; L is untouched. After line 1: L = [15 10 5], M = [17 12 7].
dincrList walks L’s own nodes adding 1 to each and returns the same arrow it was given.
So L = [16 11 6], N points to L’s first node; M is a separate chain and stays [17 12 7].

blocks.title: Aliasing puzzle (draw it)
blocks.prompt: IntList A = new IntList(1, new IntList(2, new IntList(3, null))); IntList B = A.rest; B.first = 20; A.rest.rest = A; Print A.first, A.rest.first, A.rest.rest.first, B.rest.first.
steps: B → the second node. B.first = 20: A is 1 → 20 → 3.
A.rest.rest = A: the second node’s rest now points back to the first node. The 3 node is garbage; the list is the cycle 1 → 20 → 1 → 20 …
A.first = 1; A.rest.first = 20; A.rest.rest is the first node: 1; B.rest is also the first node: 1.

blocks.text: get(i) on an IntList is Θ(i) because the only way to reach node i is to follow i arrows; an array computes the address start + i·size directly, so array access is Θ(1).

blocks.title: Recipe for list recursion
items: Base case: L == null (empty list), sometimes also L.rest == null.
Trust the call on L.rest: it returns the correct answer for the rest of the list.
Destructive: set L.rest = recursiveResult and return L (or return the recursive result to drop L).
Always return the (possibly new) head, and remind callers to write L = method(L).

blocks.title: Destructively remove every occurrence of x
blocks.prompt: Write static IntList dremoveAll(IntList L, int x) without new. Trace it on L = [3 1 3 3 2 3], x = 3; also say what the variable L prints afterward.
steps: Code: if (L == null) return null; if (L.first == x) return dremoveAll(L.rest, x); L.rest = dremoveAll(L.rest, x); return L;
Node 3 (head) matches: skip it, return the answer for [1 3 3 2 3].
Node 1 does not match: its rest becomes dremoveAll([3 3 2 3]) which skips both 3s and returns the 2 node whose rest becomes dremoveAll([3]) = null.
Result: 1 → 2. The returned head is the 1 node.
The caller’s variable L still points at the old head node 3, whose rest still points at the 1 node, so L prints [3 1 2].
blocks.answer: returns [1 2]; L (not reassigned) prints [3 1 2] — always write L = dremoveAll(L, 3);

blocks.title: Iterative in-place reverse
blocks.prompt: static IntList reverse(IntList p) { IntList prev = null; while (p != null) { IntList next = p.rest; p.rest = prev; prev = p; p = next; } return prev; } Trace on R = [1 2 3]; what do reverse(R) and then R print?
steps: Start: prev = null, p = 1.
Iteration 1: next = 2, 1.rest = null, prev = 1, p = 2.
Iteration 2: next = 3, 2.rest = 1, prev = 2, p = 3.
Iteration 3: next = null, 3.rest = 2, prev = 3, p = null. Return 3.
R still points at node 1, which is now the last node (rest = null).

blocks.title: Recursive reverse
blocks.prompt: Write a recursive destructive reverse and trace the key step on [1 2 3 4].
steps: if (L == null || L.rest == null) return L; IntList r = reverse(L.rest); L.rest.rest = L; L.rest = null; return r;
Trust: reverse([2 3 4]) returns 4 → 3 → 2 and node 2 is now its last node; L.rest still points at node 2.
L.rest.rest = L hangs node 1 after node 2; L.rest = null ends the list.

blocks.title: Swap adjacent pairs, recursively and destructively
blocks.prompt: Write swapPairs so that [1 2 3 4 5] becomes [2 1 4 3 5] with no new.
steps: Base: if L == null || L.rest == null return L.
IntList second = L.rest; — the node that will become the head.
L.rest = swapPairs(second.rest); — node 1 now leads to the swapped rest [4 3 5].
second.rest = L; return second;

blocks.text: In destructive code, save p.rest before overwriting it, or the rest of the list is lost forever.

cards.front: What does y = x do in Java?

back.text: It copies the bits in box x into box y (the Golden Rule of Equals). Primitive: independent copy of the value. Reference: copy of the arrow, so both names reach the same object.

cards.front: What are the 8 primitive types?

back.text: byte, short, int, long, float, double, boolean, char. Everything else is a reference type.

cards.front: Is Java pass by value or by reference?

back.text: Always by value. For objects the value copied is an arrow, so a method can mutate the caller’s object but can never re-aim the caller’s variable.

cards.front: What does d2.binomen = "Lupus" do if binomen is static?

back.text: Writes the one static variable Dog.binomen. Every Dog (and the class) now sees "Lupus".

cards.front: Why can’t a static method use an instance variable?

back.text: There is no this: a static method is not called on any object. Compile error.

cards.front: Default value of an unassigned field vs local variable?

back.text: Fields: 0 / 0.0 / false / null. Locals have none; using one before assignment is a compile error.

cards.front: 7 / 2, -7 / 2, -7 % 3, (int) -3.99?

back.text: 3, −3, −1, −3. Integer division and casts truncate toward zero; % takes the sign of the left operand.

cards.front: 1 + 2 + "3" + 4 + 5 and 'a' + 1 + "x"?

back.text: "3345" and "98x". + is left to right; ints/chars add until a String appears.

cards.front: What does == compare for objects/arrays?

back.text: Addresses (same object?), never contents.

cards.front: What is in new Dog[3]?

back.text: An array object with three null arrows. No Dog is constructed.

cards.front: What does arr.clone() copy for an array of objects?

back.text: A shallow copy: a new array whose slots hold the same arrows. Mutating copy[i].field is visible through the original.

cards.front: What is a 2D array in Java?

back.text: An array of arrows to row arrays. Rows may have different lengths, may be null, and may be shared (m[2] = m[1]).

cards.front: Three parts of a correct recursion?

back.text: Base case answered directly; recursive case on a smaller input; every path reaches a base case.

cards.front: What causes StackOverflowError?

back.text: Recursion too deep — usually a missing base case or one the input can skip (e.g. n == 0 with n decreasing by 2).

cards.front: IntList: what is the empty list?

back.text: null. A non-empty list is a node with first and rest (another IntList or null).

cards.front: Runtime of IntList get(i) vs array a[i]?

back.text: Θ(i) (follow i arrows) vs Θ(1) (address arithmetic).

cards.front: Destructive vs non-destructive list method?

back.text: Destructive edits existing nodes and uses no new; non-destructive builds new nodes and leaves the input untouched.

cards.front: Template for a non-destructive recursive list method?

back.text: if (L == null) return null; return new IntList(f(L.first), method(L.rest));

cards.front: Template for destructively deleting nodes recursively?

back.text: if (L == null) return null; if (bad(L)) return method(L.rest); L.rest = method(L.rest); return L;

cards.front: After dremoveAll(L, x) removes the head, what does L show?

back.text: The old head node, still pointing into the list. Always write L = dremoveAll(L, x);.

cards.front: Three pointers for in-place reverse?

back.text: prev, p, next: save next = p.rest, set p.rest = prev, advance prev = p, p = next.

cards.front: After R2 = reverse(R) on [1 2 3], what is R?

back.text: [1]: R still points at the old head, which is now the tail.

cards.front: Non-destructive catenate(A, B): which nodes are shared?

back.text: A’s nodes are copied; B’s nodes are shared by the result (the copy’s last node points at B). Changing the result’s B-part changes B.

cards.front: Inside a method, L = L.rest; L.first = 100; — does the caller see it?

back.text: The reassignment no; the mutation yes. L = L.rest only re-aims the local copy, but L.first = 100 changes a real node in the caller’s list.

cards.front: What does 'b' - 'a' evaluate to?

back.text: The int 1 (chars are numbers).

prompt.text: Write static IntList removeAll(IntList L, int x) that destructively removes every node whose first is x and returns the new head. Constraints: no recursion, no new, Θ(n) time. It must work when the list is empty, when all nodes match, and when matches are adjacent. What does it return for [3 3 1 3 2 3 3] and for [3 3] with x = 3?

solution.text: Invariant: p always holds a value ≠ x, so we only ever look one ahead and splice. The key detail is not advancing p after a splice, so that adjacent matches (3 3) are both removed.

On [3 3 1 3 2 3 3]: the head loop skips two 3s, L = 1. p = 1: next is 3 → splice (1 → 2); next is 2 → advance p = 2; next 3 → splice; next 3 → splice; p.rest = null, stop. Returns [1 2]. On [3 3] the first loop empties the list and returns null. Both verified by running.

prompt.text: Write a destructive static IntList squash(IntList L): scanning left to right, whenever two adjacent nodes have equal values, replace them by one node holding the sum; a node produced by merging is never merged again. No new. Give the output for [2 2 2 4 4 8 8 8], [2 2 4] and [1 1 1 1].

solution.text: Recursing on L.rest.rest after a merge is what guarantees the merged node is final: [2 2 4] gives 4 then [4] → [4 4], not [8].

prompt.text: Write static IntList[] split(IntList L) that destructively rearranges L’s nodes into two lists — positions 0, 2, 4, … and positions 1, 3, 5, … — and returns them as a length-2 array. Use recursion, no new IntList. Output for [1 2 3 4 5]?

solution.text: Key idea: relative to L.rest, every position shifts by one. So the even positions of L are L followed by the odd positions of the rest, and the odd positions of L are the even positions of the rest.

hard.title: Swap pairs and a dangling variable

prompt.text: With the recursive swapPairs (base case: fewer than 2 nodes; second = L.rest; L.rest = swapPairs(second.rest); second.rest = L; return second;), run IntList SP = [1 2 3 4 5]; IntList SP2 = swapPairs(SP);. What do SP2 and SP print?

solution.text: SP2 is the swapped list 2 → 1 → 4 → 3 → 5.
SP was never reassigned, so it still points at the node holding 1. In the new list that node sits second, and following it gives 1 → 4 → 3 → 5.
Lesson: a destructive method that changes the head forces the caller to reassign. Verified by running.

hard.title: Rotate right by k in place

prompt.text: Write static IntList rotateRight(IntList L, int k) (k ≥ 0, possibly larger than the length) that moves the last k nodes to the front, destructively, in Θ(n), no new. Outputs for ([1 2 3 4 5], 2), ([1 2 3], 3), ([1 2 3], 4)?

solution.text: One pass finds n and the last node; reduce k mod n; the new tail is node n − k − 1. Cut after it and hang the old list after the old last node. k = 3 on length 3 reduces to 0 (no change); k = 4 reduces to 1. Verified by running.

hard.title: What would Java print: mutation vs re-aiming in a method

solution.text: Local L starts at node 1 (copy of the arrow). L = L.rest: local L → node 2 (caller unaffected).
L.first = 100: mutates node 2, which is in the caller’s list: 1 → 100 → 3 → 4.
L = new IntList(7, L): a new node 7 whose rest is node 2; local L → 7. Caller unaffected.
L.rest.rest = null: L.rest is node 2; its rest becomes null — a real mutation. Caller’s list is now 1 → 100.
Output [1 100] (verified).
p1.shared[0] = 5 writes the single static array; later Pt.shared = new int[]{8, 8} re-aims the single static variable, so every instance now reads 8.
p2.mine = p1.mine aliases p1’s instance array; p2.mine[1] = 7 is visible as p1.mine[1] = 7.
p1.x = 3 sets only p1’s field; p2.x is still 0.
p2.y = 4 sets static y; p1.y++ makes it 5; Pt.y is the same box. Output 8 7 0 5 5 (verified).

prompt.text: With the non-destructive catenate(A, B) (copies A’s nodes, returns B when A is null) and the destructive dcatenate(A, B) (sets the last rest of A to B), run: X = [1 2]; Y = [3 4]; Z = catenate(X, Y); Z.rest.rest.first = 30; X2 = [1 2]; Z2 = dcatenate(X2, Y);. Give X, Y, Z, whether Z.rest.rest == Y, then X2 and whether Z2 == X2.

solution.text: catenate copies 1 and 2 but its base case returns B itself, so the copy of 2 points at Y’s first node. Z.rest.rest is Y’s head, so setting its first to 30 changes Y to [30 4]. X is untouched.
dcatenate walks X2’s own nodes and sets the 2-node’s rest to Y: X2 becomes [1 2 30 4] and the function returns X2 itself.
All four lines verified by running. “Non-destructive” only promises not to change A; it may still share B.

hard.title: Write a non-destructive reverse in Θ(n)

prompt.text: Write static IntList reverseND(IntList L) that returns a reversed copy without changing L, in Θ(n) time. Why is the obvious “reverse the rest then catenate the first at the end” version slower?

hard.answer: Prepend each item to an accumulator; the catenate version is Θ(n²)

solution.text: Walking L front to back and prepending builds the reversal: [1 2 3] gives 1, then 2 → 1, then 3 → 2 → 1. L is untouched (verified: L = [1 2 3], result [3 2 1]).
reverse(rest) + [first] copies a list of length n−1, n−2, …: total Θ(n²).

hard.title: A skippable base case

prompt.text: Consider static int g(int n) { calls++; if (n <= 0) return 0; return n + g(n - 2); } with a static counter. What are g(7) and the number of calls? What goes wrong if the base case is written n == 0, and what is the runtime of g in terms of n?

hard.answer: g(7) = 16 with 5 calls; n == 0 overflows the stack for odd n; Θ(n)

solution.text: With n == 0, odd inputs go 1 → −1 → −3 … never reaching 0: StackOverflowError.
About n/2 + 1 calls, each Θ(1): Θ(n).

keyFacts: GRoE: y = x copies bits; references copy the arrow, so both names reach one object.
Java is pass-by-value: a method can mutate the caller’s object but never re-aim the caller’s variable.
Static = one copy per class (writing through any instance changes it for all); instance = one per object.
== compares addresses for objects and arrays; use equals / Arrays.equals for contents.
Integer / and casts truncate toward 0; % takes the sign of the left side; + is left to right (string once a String appears).
new Dog[3] is three null arrows; clone() of an object array is shallow.
Destructive = no new, edits nodes; caller must write L = f(L) if the head can change.
List recursion: base case null; trust f(L.rest); non-destructive returns new IntList(…, f(L.rest)); destructive sets L.rest = f(L.rest).
IntList get(i) is Θ(i); array access Θ(1).
